newsitem.title: USA: Tropical Storm Hortense near Guadeloupe.
newsitem.headline: Tropical Storm Hortense near Guadeloupe.

text.p: A hurricane warning was issued for the British and U.S. Virgin Islands on Saturday night as Tropical Storm Hortense passed over the French Island of Guadeloupe in the eastern Caribbean, the National Hurricane Centre said.
Tropical storm warnings remained in effect for the northeastern Caribbean from Martinique westward to Saint Maarten, and a tropical storm warning and hurricane watch were posted for Puerto Rico.

A hurricane or tropical storm warning indicates that hurricane or tropical storm conditions, respectively, are expected within 24 hours. Hurricane and tropical storm watches are posted 36 hours ahead of possible landfall.
Additionally, forecasters warned that residents of the Dominican Republic, Haiti and the Turks & Caicos Islands should keep a close eye on Hortense.
At 11 p.m. EDT (0300 GMT), Hortense's centre was located very near the tip of Guadeloupe, at latitude 16.3 north and longitude 61.8 west.

The storm carried maximum sustained winds of about 65 mph (105 kph) and was moving west-northwest at 10 mph (16 kph), a track that forecasters said was expected to continue for the next 24 hours and would bring Hortense's centre into the northeastern Caribbean on Sunday. Further strengthening also was likely by Sunday evening, the National Hurricane Centre said.
Hortense would become a hurricane if sustained winds reached 74 mph (119 kmh).
Hortense gathered strength in the wake of Hurricane Fran, which hit the U.S. coast on Thursday, wreaking havoc through the Carolinas and killing at least 22 people.
Hortense was upgraded to tropical storm status at mid-morning on Saturday.

The string of tiny Leeward Islands -- including Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe, Antigua, Montserrat, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the British Virgin Islands -- immediately issued tropical storm warnings and urged residents to prepare.
Forecasters said it was too early to predict whether Hortense would threaten the U.S. mainland.

"It's way too early to know if the continental United States is going to be affected. There's so much time that any number of factors could turn it away," said Ed Rappaport of the National Hurricane Centre.
Early next week Hortense was expected to be near Haiti and the Dominican Republic, which share the island of Hispaniola. The island is about 700 miles (1,125 km) south of Florida.
Tropical storm force winds extended outward up to 85 miles (140 km) east of the centre.
Hortense was also dumping rain of up to 10 inches (25 cm) along its path. Forecasters warned that even more rain could fall as Hortense moved over mountains, increasing the risk of flash floods.
